                       UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                           
6                    WESTERN DISTRICT OF WASHINGTON                           
                               AT SEATTLE                                     
7                                                                             
     STEVEN FLOYD,                   CASE NO. C22-1599-KKE                    
8                                                                             

                   Plaintiff(s),     ORDER GRANTING MOTION FOR                
9                                                                             
          v.                         LEAVE TO AMEND                           

10                                                                             
     AMAZON.COM INC., et al.,                                                 

11                                                                             
                    Defendant(s).                                             

12                                                                             
         This matter comes before the Court on a motion for leave to amend the complaint, filed by 
13                                                                             
    Plaintiff’s class counsel.  Dkt. No. 80.  The Court has considered the parties’ briefing,1 the oral 
14                                                                             
    argument of counsel, and the remainder of the record.  For the reasons explained herein, the Court 
15                                                                             
    grants the motion for leave to amend.                                     
16                                                                             
                            I.  BACKGROUND                                    
17                                                                             
         Plaintiff Steven Floyd filed this putative class action in November 2022, alleging that the 
18                                                                             
    Global Tenets Agreement between Defendants Apple Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. violates Section 
19                                                                             
    1 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1.  Dkt. No. 1.  Defendants filed motions to dismiss in February 
20                                                                             
    2023 (Dkt. Nos. 30, 32), and Floyd filed an amended complaint in response (Dkt. No. 37).  
21                                                                             
    Defendants filed another round of motions to dismiss in March 2023 (Dkt. Nos. 42, 43), which 
22                                                                             
    were granted in part and denied in part in June 2023.  See Dkt. No. 61.   
23                                                                             

24   1 This order refers to the parties’ briefing using the CM/ECF page numbers. 
1        Since then, the parties have worked to resolve discovery-related disputes, some of which 
2   have warranted Court intervention.  See Dkt. Nos. 53, 70, 74, 77.  In February 2024, class counsel 
3   filed a motion to amend the complaint to add class representatives because Floyd “recently ceased 

4   responding to inquiries from counsel for the proposed class[.]”  Dkt. No. 80 at 5.  The motion 
5   proposes  amending  the  complaint  to  list  Jolene  Furdek  and  Jonathan  Ryan  as  new  class 
6   representatives asserting the same Sherman Act claim, on the same facts alleged in the first 
7   amended  complaint.    Id.;  Dkt.  No.  81-4.  The proposed  amended  complaint  also  omits  the 
8   allegations that were dismissed in the order granting in part the motions to dismiss, without 
9   waiving the right to challenge the dismissal on appeal.  See Dkt. No. 81-4 at 14 n.15.   
10        Defendants oppose the motion for leave to amend on a variety of grounds (Dkt. No. 86), 
11   but for the following reasons, the Court grants the motion.               
12                             II.  ANALYSIS                                   

13   A.   Legal Standards                                                      
14        A party may amend its pleading once as a matter of course, and thereafter “only with the 
15   opposing party’s written consent or the court’s leave.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2).  “The court should 
16   freely give leave when justice so requires.”  Id.  A court “considers the following five factors to 
17   assess whether to grant leave to amend: (1) bad faith, (2) undue delay, (3) prejudice to the opposing 
18   party, (4) futility of amendment; and (5) whether plaintiff has previously amended his complaint.”  
19   In re W. States Wholesale Nat. Gas Antitrust Litig., 715 F.3d 716, 738 (9th Cir. 2013) (cleaned 
20   up), aff’d sub nom. Oneok, Inc. v. Learjet, Inc., 575 U.S. 373 (2015).  “The opposing party bears 
21   the burden to show why leave to amend should not be granted.”  Robertson v. Bruckert, 568 F. 
22   Supp. 3d 1044, 1047 (N.D. Cal. 2021).                                     

23        If a court’s scheduling order sets forth a deadline for amending the pleadings, no post-
24   deadline amendment is permitted unless the court first finds good cause to amend the case 
1   schedule.  See Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(4); Kamal v. Eden Creamery, LLC, 88 F.4th 1268, 1277 (9th 
2   Cir. 2023).  Good cause exists where the moving party is diligent in requesting a modification.  
3   Johnson v. Mammoth Recreations, Inc., 975 F.2d 604, 607–09 (9th Cir. 1992).   

4        “Although the existence or degree of prejudice to the party opposing the modification 
5   might supply additional reasons to deny a motion [for leave to amend], the focus of the inquiry is 
6   upon the moving party’s reasons for seeking modification,” and “[i]f that party was not diligent, 
7   the inquiry should end.”  Johnson, 975 F.2d at 609.                       
8        To demonstrate diligence under Rule 16’s “good cause” standard, the movant may 
         be required to show the following: (1) that he was diligent in assisting the court in 
9        creating a workable Rule 16 order; (2) that his noncompliance with a Rule 16 
         deadline occurred or will occur, notwithstanding his diligent efforts to comply, 
10        because of the development of matters which could not have been reasonably 
         foreseen or anticipated at the time of the Rule 16 scheduling conference; and (3) 
11        that he was diligent in seeking amendment of the Rule 16 order, once it became 
         apparent that he could not comply with the order.                    
12                                                                             
    Morgal v. Maricopa Cnty. Bd. of Supervisors, 284 F.R.D. 452, 460 (D. Ariz. 2012) (cleaned up).  
13                                                                             
    “Only after the moving party has demonstrated diligence under Rule 16 does the court apply the 
14                                                                             
    standard under Rule 15 to determine whether the amendment [is] proper.”  Hood v. Hartford Life 
15                                                                             
    & Accident Ins. Co., 567 F. Supp. 2d 1221, 1224 (E.D. Cal. 2008).         
16                                                                             
         “To permit a party to disregard a Rule 16 order by an appeal to the standards of Rule 
17                                                                             
    15 would ‘undermine the court’s ability to control its docket, disrupt the agreed-upon course of 
18                                                                             
    the litigation, and reward the indolent and the cavalier.’”  Eckert Cold Storage, Inc. v. Behl, 943 
19                                                                             
    F. Supp. 1230, 1233 (E.D. Cal. 1996) (quoting Johnson, 975 F.2d at 610–11).  A determination of 
20                                                                             
    whether good cause exists to modify a case schedule is committed to the broad discretion of the 
21                                                                             
    district court.  See C.F. ex rel. Farman v. Capistrano Unified Sch. Dist., 654 F.3d 975, 984 (9th 
22                                                                             
    Cir. 2011).                                                               
23                                                                             

24                                                                             
1   B.   Adjudication of Plaintiff’s Adequacy as a Class Representative is Premature. 

2        Before turning to consider the motion for leave to amend under the applicable Federal 
3   Rules of Civil Procedure, the Court first addresses Defendants’ primary argument in opposition, 
4   which is that Floyd is an inadequate named Plaintiff.  Specifically, Defendants argue that because 
5   Floyd was never qualified to represent the class in the first place, “[s]ubjecting Defendants to the 
6   burdens of litigation for over a year with a plaintiff who is an inadequate representative of the 
7   putative class, while simultaneously refusing to produce documents or offer dates for deposition, 
8   is conduct that makes amendment inappropriate.”  Dkt. No. 86 at 10.  According to Defendants, 
9   the motion to amend is not simply a motion to add or substitute a class representative, but should 
10   be considered a “back-door attempt to begin the action anew.”  Id. (quoting Lidie v. State of Cal., 
11   478 F.2d 552, 555 (9th Cir. 1973)).                                       
12        But whether Floyd is an adequate representative of the putative class is not before the Court 

13   at this point in the litigation, and Defendants will have an opportunity to fully litigate this issue in 
14   the context of a motion for class certification.  Defendants have not shown that Floyd’s potential 
15   inadequacy as a class representative is an inherent defect in his party status akin to a lack of 
16   standing or mootness, such that there is no live case or controversy before the Court.  In the absence 
17   of an inherent defect in Floyd’s claims, the Court will allow amendment of the complaint to add 
18   additional named plaintiffs.  See, e.g., Kirby v. McMenamins Inc., C22-5168-BHS-MLP, 2023 WL 
19   4623988 (W.D. Wash. July 19, 2023); Fife v. Sci. Games Corp., No. 2:18-cv-00565-RBL, 2020 
20   WL 4933959, at *1–2 (W.D. Wash. Aug. 24, 2020) (finding that a putative class action is not 
21   mooted when a sole named plaintiff seeks to withdraw for personal reasons but can be replaced 
22   immediately); Castillo v. United Rentals (N. Am.), Inc., No. C17-1573JLR, 2018 WL 3429936, at 

23   *3 (W.D. Wash. July 16, 2018) (permitting a pre-certification substitution of the named plaintiff 
24                                                                             
1   where the current sole named plaintiff’s claims persist (had not been settled or dismissed), and 
2   counsel could produce a substitute immediately).                          
3        The absence of an adjudication of Floyd’s adequacy distinguishes this case from cases cited 

4   by Defendants.  For example, Defendants rely on Lidie, 478 F.2d at 555, where the Ninth Circuit 
5   upheld a denial of a motion to intervene because, “where the original plaintiffs were never qualified 
6   to represent the class, a motion to intervene represents a back-door attempt to begin the action 
7   anew, and need not be granted.”  But here, Floyd has not been found unqualified to represent the 
8   putative  class.    Although  Defendants  vigorously  dispute  Floyd’s  adequacy  as  a  class 
9   representative, the Court finds that it would be premature to adjudicate this issue in the context of 
10   a motion for leave to amend.                                              
11        Likewise, Defendants ask the Court to follow Miller v. Mercedes-Benz USA LLC, No. CV 
12   06-0532 ABC (JTLX), 2009 WL 1393488, at *1–2 (C.D. Cal. May 15, 2009), but in that case, the 

13   sole named plaintiff included in her motion for class certification a request to add an additional 
14   named plaintiff to cure her own conflict of interest in serving as a class representative.  The Miller 
15   court denied the current named plaintiff’s motion for class certification because she could not fairly 
16   and adequately protect the interests of the class, and found that her last-minute attempt to add a 
17   named plaintiff was a “bait-and-switch tactic.”  Id. at *2.  Miller is distinguishable from this case 
18   because the motion before that court requested class certification, which required the court to 
19   determine whether the sole named plaintiff was an adequate representative.  This case has not 
20   proceeded to that stage of litigation, and the Court declines to consider issues now, on this record 
21   and with limited briefing, that it will have the opportunity to consider in full at class certification. 
22   C.   There is Good Cause to Amend the Case Schedule.                      

23        The Court now considers whether the motion for leave to amend should be granted under 
24   the applicable Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.  First, the Court must resolve the parties’ dispute 
1   as  to  whether  Rule  15  (addressing  leave  to  amend  pleadings)  and/or  Rule  16  (addressing 
2   modifications to a case schedule) applies to the motion.                  
3        Here, the case schedule does not set out a deadline for either amending pleadings or adding 

4   parties, but sets deadlines only as to substantial completion of productions, fact discovery cutoff, 
5   disclosure of expert reports, and the briefing of a class-certification motion.  See Dkt. No. 68.  
6   Although the motion for leave to amend the complaint is therefore not technically untimely under 
7   this case schedule, Defendants nonetheless contend that the motion for leave to amend should be 
8   considered under Rule 16 because granting it would necessitate modifying the scheduling order: 
9   the deadlines for substantial completion of productions (April 3, 2024) and the fact discovery 
10   cutoff (July 8, 2024) cannot be met if the complaint is amended.  Dkt. No. 86 at 12.  Defendants 
11   argue that even if class counsel agrees to treat all discovery requests on Floyd as if they had been 
12   served on the new representatives, as counsel has offered, Defendants would still want to serve 

13   discovery requests tailored to the new representatives, and they would not have been able to 
14   respond to those requests by April 3.  Id.                                
15        Indeed, while the motion for leave to amend was pending, the parties filed a stipulated 
16   motion to suspend the April 3 deadline and indicated that they will confer regarding a new case 
17   schedule after the Court has resolved all motions currently pending.  See Dkt. No. 93.  Under these 
18   circumstances, where even the filing of a motion for leave to amend has necessitated adjustment 
19   of the case schedule, the Court finds that Rule 16 applies and good cause must be shown to modify 
20   the case schedule, before the Court will consider whether the motion for leave to amend should be 
21   granted under Rule 15.  See Paz v. City of Aberdeen, No. C13-5104 RJB, 2013 WL 6163016, at 
22   *2–3 (W.D. Wash. Nov. 25, 2013).                                          

23        The good cause standard has been easily met here.  Class counsel diligently moved to 
24   substitute the new representatives after Floyd unexpectedly stopped communicating with them.  
1   Counsel last communicated with Floyd on January 16, 2024 (Dkt. No. 81-1 at 2) and moved to 
2   amend the complaint on February 29, 2024.  Dkt. No. 80.  That span of time reflects diligence.  
3   See, e.g., Kirby, 2023 WL 4623988, at *4 (finding that counsel had been diligent in bringing the 

4   motion for leave to amend less than two months after receiving contact information for putative 
5   class members and less than a month after the new class representatives expressed interest in 
6   becoming class representatives and retained counsel).  Moreover, amendment permits this case to 
7   move forward after Floyd apparently lost interest in continuing to participate, which constitutes 
8   good cause for amendment.  See Fife, 2020 WL 4933959, at *3.              
9        Defendants suggest that counsel was not diligent in selecting Floyd as a named plaintiff in 
10   the first place, because counsel should have known from this case’s inception (or at least since the 
11   motions to dismiss were granted in part) that Floyd does not adequately represent the class due to 
12   his shopping behavior.  Dkt. No. 86 at 14–15.  Accepting this argument would require the Court 

13   to consider Floyd’s adequacy as a class representative prematurely.  Again, Floyd’s adequacy as a 
14   class representative has not been adjudicated to date and will not be adjudicated on an incomplete 
15   record in the context of this motion.                                     
16   D.   Justice Requires Leave to Amend the Complaint.                       

17        The Court has found good cause to amend the case schedule, and now turns to consider 
18   whether the motion for leave to amend the complaint should be granted under Rule 15.  As noted 
19   above, Defendants bear the burden of showing that justice requires denying the motion for leave 
20   to amend.  Defendants contend that the motion should be denied in light of undue delay and 
21   prejudice, but for the following reasons, the Court disagrees.            
22        1.  Undue Delay                                                      
23        First, Defendants argue that class counsel unduly delayed in seeking amendment because 
24   they should have known earlier that Floyd was an inadequate class representative.  Dkt. No. 86 at 
1   14–15.  As stated supra, that is not the grounds upon which amendment is requested, and the Court 
2   will not assume Floyd’s inadequacy as a class representative simply because Defendants assert it, 
3   nor will the Court adjudicate that issue without the benefit of full briefing.  Because Defendants 

4   have not identified a point in this litigation where Floyd’s inadequacy as a class representative was 
5   made plain to class counsel, the Court will not start the diligence clock running at a point earlier 
6   than the time when Floyd stopped communicating with counsel.  And for the reasons stated supra 
7   with respect to Rule 16, and the Court finds that counsel was diligent in filing this motion after 
8   that time.                                                                
9        2.  Prejudice                                                        
10        Second, Defendants argue that they would be prejudiced via the need to conduct new and/or 
11   additional discovery that would not otherwise have been required had class counsel identified the 
12   appropriate representatives in the first instance.  Dkt. No. 86 at 14.  Given that the parties have 

13   recently agreed to suspend the discovery deadlines and discovery has not even closed under the 
14   original  deadlines,  Defendants  have  not  shown  that  permitting  amendment  would  lead  to 
15   substantial prejudice.  The cases Defendants cite to support a finding of undue prejudice involve 
16   amendments sought after discovery had closed or after a motion for class certification was filed.  
17   See Paz, 2013 WL 6163016, at *4; In re Flash Memory Antitrust Litig., No. C 07-0086 SBA, 2010 
18   WL 2332081, at *17 (N.D. Cal. June 9, 2010).                              
19        Defendants also argue that the amendments are intended to “circumvent a potentially fatal 
20   statute of limitations issue” and that Defendants “would be prejudiced by having to defend against 
21   an untimely putative class action.”  Dkt. No. 86 at 13.  Defendants state that they did not raise this 
22   issue in their motions to dismiss because resolving it requires deposing Floyd.  Id. at 13 n.3.  But 

23   this issue is not squarely before the Court, and has not been briefed, given that Floyd has not yet 
24   been deposed.  The Court again declines to wade into substantive issues prematurely, without the 
1   benefit of full briefing and an adequate record, and the Court cannot find that Defendants are 
2   prejudiced by having to defend this case while its timeliness is still an open question. 
3        For all of these reasons, the Court finds that the motion for leave to amend is supported by 

4   good cause and that Defendants have not shown that justice requires its denial.  Because leave to 
5   amend the complaint is granted, the motion to intervene in the alternative (Dkt. No. 80 at 14–16) 
6   is denied as moot.                                                        
7   E.   The Parties Shall Confer Regarding a New Case Schedule.              
8        Defendants request that if the Court grants leave to amend, the Court should also  
9        stay discovery as to the Defendants for 90 days (and suspend the extant substantial 
         completion deadline) to further the just and efficient resolution of this case.…  This 
10        will allow Defendants to take initial discovery of the new  representatives to 
         determine if there is even a viable plaintiff in this case, and to establish amendment 
11        would  not  be  futile.    After  the  new  representatives  (or  Floyd)  meet  their 
         corresponding discovery obligations, then Defendants should have the opportunity 
12        to file a dispositive motion or continue with discovery on a revised schedule. 

13   Dkt. No. 86 at 16.  Class counsel’s reply objects to a discovery stay that would apply to Defendants 
14   only, noting that Defendants “have not produced a single responsive document” to date.  Dkt. No. 
15   92 at 10.                                                                 
16        As noted supra, after Defendants’ opposition to the motion for leave to amend was filed, 
17   the parties filed a stipulated motion to suspend the case schedule until after the Court resolved the 
18   pending motions.  See Dkt. No. 93.  The parties agreed that they would confer regarding a new 
19   case schedule and, if necessary, set out a briefing schedule on a contested motion to modify the 
20   schedule.  Id.  Thus, at this time, the Court finds that Defendants’ concern in their opposition 
21   regarding the case schedule has been mooted by the subsequent stipulation.  Defendants will have 
22   an opportunity to address any concerns about schedule revisions either when conferring with class 
23   counsel or when briefing a contested motion to modify the case schedule, if one is necessary. 
24   //                                                                        
1                           III.  CONCLUSION                                  
2        For these reasons, the Court GRANTS the motion for leave to amend.  Dkt. No. 80.  A 
3   second amended complaint shall be filed no later than May 10, 2024.       

4        The parties shall confer regarding case schedule modification and whether the statement of 
5   discovery disputes filed on March 26, 2024 (Dkt. No. 90) should be re-briefed in light of this order.  
6   The parties shall file either a stipulation on these issues or set forth a briefing schedule on these 
7   issues, no later than May 13, 2024.  The clerk is directed to terminate the dispute (Dkt. No. 90) at 
8   this time, subject to reactivation by the Court after reviewing the parties’ submission. 
9        Plaintiffs are also granted leave to file a motion to compel with regard to the disputes 
10   outlined in the joint statement filed on March 22, 2024.  Dkt. No. 89.  As discussed at the discovery 
11   conference, the Court finds that the issues to be resolved in that statement of disputes warrants full 
12   briefing.  The clerk is directed to terminate the dispute (Dkt. No. 89) as a motion at this time.   

13        Dated this 6th day of May, 2024.                                     
14                                                                             
                                  A                                           
15                                                                             
                                  Kymberly K. Evanson                         
16                                 United States District Judge

18   additional named plaintiffs.  See, e.g., Kirby v. McMenamins Inc., C22-5168-BHS-MLP,
2023 WL 19
   4623988 (W.D. Wash. July 19, 2023); Fife v. Sci. Games Corp., No. 2:18-cv-00565-RBL, 2020
20 WL 4933959
, at *1–2 (W.D. Wash. Aug. 24, 2020) (finding that a putative class action is not 
21   mooted when a sole named plaintiff seeks to withdraw for personal reasons but can be replaced 
22   immediately); Castillo v. United Rentals (N. Am.), Inc., No. C17-1573JLR,
2018 WL 3429936
, at 

23   *3 (W.D. Wash. July 16, 2018) (permitting a pre-certification substitution of the named plaintiff 
24                                                                             
1   where the current sole named plaintiff’s claims persist (had not been settled or dismissed), and 
2   counsel could produce a substitute immediately).                          
3        The absence of an adjudication of Floyd’s adequacy distinguishes this case from cases cited 

4   by Defendants.  For example, Defendants rely on Lidie,
478 F.2d at 555
, where the Ninth Circuit 
5   upheld a denial of a motion to intervene because, “where the original plaintiffs were never qualified 
6   to represent the class, a motion to intervene represents a back-door attempt to begin the action 
7   anew, and need not be granted.”  But here, Floyd has not been found unqualified to represent the 
8   putative  class.    Although  Defendants  vigorously  dispute  Floyd’s  adequacy  as  a  class 
9   representative, the Court finds that it would be premature to adjudicate this issue in the context of 
10   a motion for leave to amend.                                              
11        Likewise, Defendants ask the Court to follow Miller v. Mercedes-Benz USA LLC, No. CV 
12   06-0532 ABC (JTLX),
2009 WL 1393488
, at *1–2 (C.D. Cal. May 15, 2009), but in that case, the 

13   sole named plaintiff included in her motion for class certification a request to add an additional 
14   named plaintiff to cure her own conflict of interest in serving as a class representative.  The Miller 
15   court denied the current named plaintiff’s motion for class certification because she could not fairly 
16   and adequately protect the interests of the class, and found that her last-minute attempt to add a 
17   named plaintiff was a “bait-and-switch tactic.”
Id. at *2
.  Miller is distinguishable from this case 
18   because the motion before that court requested class certification, which required the court to 
19   determine whether the sole named plaintiff was an adequate representative.  This case has not 
20   proceeded to that stage of litigation, and the Court declines to consider issues now, on this record 
21   and with limited briefing, that it will have the opportunity to consider in full at class certification. 
22   C.   There is Good Cause to Amend the Case Schedule.                      

23        The Court now considers whether the motion for leave to amend should be granted under 
24   the applicable Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.  First, the Court must resolve the parties’ dispute 
1   as  to  whether  Rule  15  (addressing  leave  to  amend  pleadings)  and/or  Rule  16  (addressing 
2   modifications to a case schedule) applies to the motion.                  
3        Here, the case schedule does not set out a deadline for either amending pleadings or adding 

4   parties, but sets deadlines only as to substantial completion of productions, fact discovery cutoff, 
5   disclosure of expert reports, and the briefing of a class-certification motion.  See Dkt. No. 68.  
6   Although the motion for leave to amend the complaint is therefore not technically untimely under 
7   this case schedule, Defendants nonetheless contend that the motion for leave to amend should be 
8   considered under Rule 16 because granting it would necessitate modifying the scheduling order: 
9   the deadlines for substantial completion of productions (April 3, 2024) and the fact discovery 
10   cutoff (July 8, 2024) cannot be met if the complaint is amended.  Dkt. No. 86 at 12.  Defendants 
11   argue that even if class counsel agrees to treat all discovery requests on Floyd as if they had been 
12   served on the new representatives, as counsel has offered, Defendants would still want to serve 

13   discovery requests tailored to the new representatives, and they would not have been able to 
14   respond to those requests by April 3.
Id.
                                
15        Indeed, while the motion for leave to amend was pending, the parties filed a stipulated 
16   motion to suspend the April 3 deadline and indicated that they will confer regarding a new case 
17   schedule after the Court has resolved all motions currently pending.  See Dkt. No. 93.  Under these 
18   circumstances, where even the filing of a motion for leave to amend has necessitated adjustment 
19   of the case schedule, the Court finds that Rule 16 applies and good cause must be shown to modify 
20   the case schedule, before the Court will consider whether the motion for leave to amend should be 
21   granted under Rule 15.  See Paz v. City of Aberdeen, No. C13-5104 RJB,
2013 WL 6163016
, at 
22   *2–3 (W.D. Wash. Nov. 25, 2013).                                          

23        The good cause standard has been easily met here.  Class counsel diligently moved to 
24   substitute the new representatives after Floyd unexpectedly stopped communicating with them.  
1   Counsel last communicated with Floyd on January 16, 2024 (Dkt. No. 81-1 at 2) and moved to 
2   amend the complaint on February 29, 2024.  Dkt. No. 80.  That span of time reflects diligence.  
3   See, e.g., Kirby,
2023 WL 4623988
, at *4 (finding that counsel had been diligent in bringing the 

4   motion for leave to amend less than two months after receiving contact information for putative 
5   class members and less than a month after the new class representatives expressed interest in 
6   becoming class representatives and retained counsel).  Moreover, amendment permits this case to 
7   move forward after Floyd apparently lost interest in continuing to participate, which constitutes 
8   good cause for amendment.  See Fife,
2020 WL 4933959
, at *3.              
9        Defendants suggest that counsel was not diligent in selecting Floyd as a named plaintiff in 
10   the first place, because counsel should have known from this case’s inception (or at least since the 
11   motions to dismiss were granted in part) that Floyd does not adequately represent the class due to 
12   his shopping behavior.  Dkt. No. 86 at 14–15.  Accepting this argument would require the Court 

13   to consider Floyd’s adequacy as a class representative prematurely.  Again, Floyd’s adequacy as a 
14   class representative has not been adjudicated to date and will not be adjudicated on an incomplete 
15   record in the context of this motion.                                     
16   D.   Justice Requires Leave to Amend the Complaint.                       

17        The Court has found good cause to amend the case schedule, and now turns to consider 
18   whether the motion for leave to amend the complaint should be granted under Rule 15.  As noted 
19   above, Defendants bear the burden of showing that justice requires denying the motion for leave 
20   to amend.  Defendants contend that the motion should be denied in light of undue delay and 
21   prejudice, but for the following reasons, the Court disagrees.            
22        1.  Undue Delay                                                      
23        First, Defendants argue that class counsel unduly delayed in seeking amendment because 
24   they should have known earlier that Floyd was an inadequate class representative.  Dkt. No. 86 at 
1   14–15.  As stated supra, that is not the grounds upon which amendment is requested, and the Court 
2   will not assume Floyd’s inadequacy as a class representative simply because Defendants assert it, 
3   nor will the Court adjudicate that issue without the benefit of full briefing.  Because Defendants 

4   have not identified a point in this litigation where Floyd’s inadequacy as a class representative was 
5   made plain to class counsel, the Court will not start the diligence clock running at a point earlier 
6   than the time when Floyd stopped communicating with counsel.  And for the reasons stated supra 
7   with respect to Rule 16, and the Court finds that counsel was diligent in filing this motion after 
8   that time.                                                                
9        2.  Prejudice                                                        
10        Second, Defendants argue that they would be prejudiced via the need to conduct new and/or 
11   additional discovery that would not otherwise have been required had class counsel identified the 
12   appropriate representatives in the first instance.  Dkt. No. 86 at 14.  Given that the parties have 

13   recently agreed to suspend the discovery deadlines and discovery has not even closed under the 
14   original  deadlines,  Defendants  have  not  shown  that  permitting  amendment  would  lead  to 
15   substantial prejudice.  The cases Defendants cite to support a finding of undue prejudice involve 
16   amendments sought after discovery had closed or after a motion for class certification was filed.  
17   See Paz,
2013 WL 6163016
, at *4; In re Flash Memory Antitrust Litig., No. C 07-0086 SBA, 2010
18 WL 2332081
, at *17 (N.D. Cal. June 9, 2010).                              
19        Defendants also argue that the amendments are intended to “circumvent a potentially fatal 
20   statute of limitations issue” and that Defendants “would be prejudiced by having to defend against 
21   an untimely putative class action.”  Dkt. No. 86 at 13.  Defendants state that they did not raise this 
22   issue in their motions to dismiss because resolving it requires deposing Floyd.
Id.
 at 13 n.3.  But 

23   this issue is not squarely before the Court, and has not been briefed, given that Floyd has not yet 
24   been deposed.  The Court again declines to wade into substantive issues prematurely, without the 
1   benefit of full briefing and an adequate record, and the Court cannot find that Defendants are 
2   prejudiced by having to defend this case while its timeliness is still an open question. 
3        For all of these reasons, the Court finds that the motion for leave to amend is supported by 

4   good cause and that Defendants have not shown that justice requires its denial.  Because leave to 
5   amend the complaint is granted, the motion to intervene in the alternative (Dkt. No. 80 at 14–16) 
6   is denied as moot.                                                        
7   E.   The Parties Shall Confer Regarding a New Case Schedule.              
8        Defendants request that if the Court grants leave to amend, the Court should also  
9        stay discovery as to the Defendants for 90 days (and suspend the extant substantial 
         completion deadline) to further the just and efficient resolution of this case.…  This 
10        will allow Defendants to take initial discovery of the new  representatives to 
         determine if there is even a viable plaintiff in this case, and to establish amendment 
11        would  not  be  futile.    After  the  new  representatives  (or  Floyd)  meet  their 
         corresponding discovery obligations, then Defendants should have the opportunity 
12        to file a dispositive motion or continue with discovery on a revised schedule. 

13   Dkt. No. 86 at 16.  Class counsel’s reply objects to a discovery stay that would apply to Defendants 
14   only, noting that Defendants “have not produced a single responsive document” to date.  Dkt. No. 
15   92 at 10.                                                                 
16        As noted supra, after Defendants’ opposition to the motion for leave to amend was filed, 
17   the parties filed a stipulated motion to suspend the case schedule until after the Court resolved the 
18   pending motions.  See Dkt. No. 93.  The parties agreed that they would confer regarding a new 
19   case schedule and, if necessary, set out a briefing schedule on a contested motion to modify the 
20   schedule.  Id.  Thus, at this time, the Court finds that Defendants’ concern in their opposition 
21   regarding the case schedule has been mooted by the subsequent stipulation.  Defendants will have 
22   an opportunity to address any concerns about schedule revisions either when conferring with class 
23   counsel or when briefing a contested motion to modify the case schedule, if one is necessary.
